strengths: Unifies joint video-audio generation and video-audio editing into a single multimodal diffusion transformer model, eliminating separate cascaded modules or complex external fusion networks.

Well-motivated architectural design choices: native joint self-attention across video, audio, and text tokens reuses pretrained visual priors, while channel-wise conditioning for visual reference avoids explosive sequence length overhead.

The proposed mouth-area flow matching loss provides a simple yet effective inductive bias that significantly improves lip-speech synchronization (LSE-C increases from 1.39 to 6.70) without requiring dedicated lip-sync sub-networks.
Comprehensive data construction pipeline producing ~3M high-quality paired video-audio samples for both generation and instruction-driven editing.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple benchmarks (JoVABench-Gen, JoVABench-Edit, Verse-Bench, and VBench) along with user studies and thorough diagnostic ablations.
weaknesses: While the unification and engineering execution are strong, several key building blocks (Waver backbone, Wan2.1 VAE, MMAudio VAE, temporally aligned RoPE) are adapted from existing literature; the conceptual novelty of joint self-attention and channel concatenation is somewhat incremental.
Video-audio editing is currently limited to human speech scenarios due to training data limitations for general scenes, as acknowledged by the authors.

Baseline comparisons for editing rely on stitched cascaded pipelines (e.g., OmniVideo/Ditto + Diff2Lip/Wav2Lip) using ground-truth audio, which may suffer from compounding visual domain shifts, making direct architectural comparison somewhat indirect.
Details regarding computational resources, training compute/hardware (GPU type and wall-clock training time), and inference latency are missing.

strengths: Unified and streamlined framework: JoVA effectively unifies text-to-video-audio generation, reference-conditioned generation, pure video editing, and joint video-audio editing within a single architecture, bypassing fragmented cascaded pipelines and complex cross-modal fusion modules.

Well-motivated architectural designs: The use of native joint self-attention across video, audio, and text tokens enables seamless bidirectional interaction while directly leveraging pretrained backbone parameters. The combination of channel-wise conditioning for visual references and token concatenation for audio effectively prevents sequence length explosion.

Effective mouth-area loss: The localized mouth-area supervision in the VAE latent space directly addresses the spatial imbalance of talking-head scenarios (~2.3% frame area), yielding dramatic improvements in lip-speech synchronization (LSE-C increasing from 1.39 to 6.70 in the ablation).

Comprehensive data construction: The paper develops a scalable data curation and synthesis pipeline covering ~3M video-audio-text pairs, including rigorous filtering, multi-level annotations, and structured multi-modal edit instructions.

Extensive evaluation: Quantitative benchmarks (JoVABench-Gen, JoVABench-Edit, Verse-Bench, and VBench) alongside human subjective studies demonstrate superior performance over existing joint video-audio models and cascaded editing baselines.
weaknesses: Limited coverage of general-scene joint editing: As acknowledged by the authors, joint video-audio editing is predominantly trained and evaluated on human-speech scenarios due to paired data constraints, leaving open-domain non-speech editing largely unaddressed.

Potential bias from the synthetic editing pipeline: The paired editing data relies on a multi-stage synthetic chain (GPT-4o, FLUX.1, Wan2.2-Fun, Qwen3, Higgs-Audio, and lip-sync tools), which may inherit cumulative synthetic artifacts or limit instruction diversity.

Missing details on computational and inference efficiency: Training a 12B parameter model with joint self-attention on long video-audio sequences is computationally demanding. The paper would benefit from reporting the hardware requirements, training hours, and inference latency/memory footprint compared to baseline methods.

strengths: Comprehensive unification: JoVA successfully integrates text-to-video-audio generation, reference-image-conditioned generation, video editing, and joint video-audio editing into a unified transformer-based diffusion architecture, moving away from fragmented, multi-stage pipelines.

Well-engineered architecture and losses: The use of native joint self-attention (reusing video backbone weights for audio) and channel-wise visual conditioning elegantly avoids separate cross-attention parameters and sequence explosion. The latent-space mouth-area loss effectively resolves the spatial imbalance inherent to talking-head generation without architectural changes.

Substantial data and benchmark contribution: The authors curate a multi-domain corpus of ~3M pairs, including an automated synthesis pipeline for paired audio-video editing, and introduce two standardized benchmarks (JoVABench-Gen and JoVABench-Edit).

Thorough quantitative and human evaluation: JoVA is rigorously evaluated across multiple benchmarks (JoVABench, Verse-Bench, and VBench) and supported by extensive human user studies (MOS) and diagnostic ablations (e.g., loss weight sensitivity and comparison against sequential/parallel cross-attention designs).
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: Many individual technical components are direct adaptations or combinations of established techniques (e.g., joint multi-modal self-attention popularized in MM-DiT, channel concatenation as used in InstructPix2Pix/VACE, and spatially masked loss reweighting), which makes the overall conceptual novelty somewhat modest.

Heavy reliance on synthetic cascade for editing data: The paired editing training corpus relies on a multi-model synthetic pipeline (GPT-4o + FLUX.1 + Wan2.2-Control + Qwen3 + Higgs-Audio + external lip-sync). Potential artifacts, distributional drifts, and synthetic biases introduced by these generative backbones are not thoroughly analyzed or audited.

Limited coverage of non-speech audio editing: While the framework claims joint audio-video editing, the editing experiments and dataset are predominantly restricted to human talking-head scenarios. Editing natural audio and ambient environmental soundscapes remains largely unaddressed.

Missing hardware and computational efficiency details: Training a 12B transformer on high-resolution multimodal data is computationally heavy, yet the manuscript lacks details on training hardware, GPU hours, and inference latency/VRAM footprint compared to modular baselines.

strengths: Clear motivation and architectural simplicity: Rather than relying on complicated cross-modal fusion bridges or separate cascaded pipelines, the proposed JoVA utilizes full joint self-attention across video, audio, and text tokens within the transformer blocks.

Effective and practical solution to lip synchronization: The authors identify a crucial failure mode of generic full self-attention in joint video-audio modeling—namely, the extreme spatial and temporal sparsity of mouth movements relative to the full multimodal sequence. The proposed mouth-aware loss is simple, computationally lightweight, and remarkably effective (improving LSE-C from 1.39 to 6.64).

Thorough experimental validation: Experiments cover both avatar-specific (UniAvatar-Bench) and general video-audio benchmarks (Verse-Bench). Evaluations comprehensively assess joint synchronization (LSE-C), speech intelligibility (WER), audio quality (FD, KL, CLAP, PQ), and video quality (MS, AS, ID).

Insightful diagnostic analyses: The ablation studies clearly validate the necessity of the mouth-aware loss weight, examine the trade-offs of temporally aligned RoPE, compare different attention fusion paradigms, and demonstrate performance across model scales (3.2B and 24B total parameters).
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The unified multimodal transformer architecture mostly follows the standard single-stream / MM-DiT design paradigm, and the primary algorithmic addition is an $L_2$ flow-matching loss reweighting over the spatial-temporal mouth mask.

Lack of user study: For generative video-audio and talking-face synthesis, automated metrics (such as LSE-C, WER, and aesthetic scores) do not always correlate perfectly with human perception. A subjective Mean Opinion Score (MOS) study evaluating lip synchronization, audio realism, and overall visual fidelity would significantly reinforce the findings.

Computational complexity analysis is missing: Concatenating video, audio, and text tokens into a shared self-attention layer inherently incurs quadratic complexity with respect to the combined sequence length. The paper would benefit from reporting training/inference latency, peak memory footprints, and FLOPs compared to dual-branch / cross-attention baselines.

Minor presentation issues and typos: On page 1, the 'Project page:' URL is blank; on page 12, the Declaration section contains an unfinished sentence ('...products of .'); and on page 8 below Table 2, the text states that JoVA's LSE-C of 6.51 'slightly underperforms OVI (6.41)' while OVI's score in Table 2 is actually 6.61.

strengths: The paper promotes architectural simplicity by relying on joint self-attention over concatenated multimodal tokens rather than introducing specialized, modality-specific bridging or cross-attention modules.

The proposed mouth-aware loss is an intuitive, training-only inductive bias that effectively resolves the sparse cross-modal correspondence issue for lip synchronization without introducing runtime overhead.

The paper is well-structured and easy to follow, providing clear diagrams, concise mathematical formulations, and thorough diagnostic studies (e.g., impact of the loss weight λ, TA-RoPE, and attention variants).

Empirical results across UniAvatar-Bench and Verse-Bench demonstrate strong performance, achieving competitive or state-of-the-art results in lip-sync accuracy (LSE-C) and speech recognition accuracy (WER) compared to recent joint models such as Universe-1 and OVI.
weaknesses: The core conceptual novelty is relatively incremental: concatenating multimodal tokens within a shared transformer self-attention block is a established paradigm in diffusion transformers, and region-weighted loss on facial bounding boxes is a well-known heuristic in talking-head generation.

Computational overhead and parameter scaling: While marketed as simple, duplicating the 12B backbone leads to a 24B parameter system, and concatenating video and audio tokens inside full self-attention incurs quadratic complexity with respect to the combined sequence length. The paper would benefit from reporting training and inference throughput (e.g., latency, memory footprint, FLOPs) compared to cross-attention baselines.

The test benchmark UniAvatar-Bench contains only 100 samples, which is quite small. Testing on established public talking-head evaluation sets (e.g., HDTF or VoxCeleb2) would provide more standardized and convincing evidence.

Absence of human perceptual evaluation: Given the perceptual nature of audio-visual synchrony, natural facial dynamics, and speech naturalness, relying solely on automated metrics (e.g., SyncNet, Whisper WER, and aesthetic scores) can be insufficient; a user study (MOS or A/B testing) would significantly reinforce the claims.

strengths: Architectural simplicity and elegance: JoVA eliminates complex modality-specific fusion modules and cross-attention stacks by utilizing a unified joint self-attention mechanism across video, audio, and text tokens, adhering closely to the scalable transformer paradigm.

Targeted and practical solution for lip-speech synchronization: The mouth-aware supervision strategy specifically targets the under-represented mouth region in latent space via keypoint detection and spatio-temporal pooling, directly addressing the sparsity of cross-modal alignment signals.

Thorough quantitative evaluation: The model is comprehensively evaluated against both joint video-audio frameworks (Universe-1, OVI) and specialized audio-driven talking-face methods (Wan-S2V, FantasyTalking) across four axes: video quality, audio quality, text-to-speech accuracy (WER), and audio-visual synchronization (LSE-C).

Informative ablation studies: The paper provides clear diagnostic analyses isolating the impact of the mouth-aware loss weight (Table 3), temporal-aligned RoPE (Table 4), and joint self-attention versus cross-attention variants (Table 5), alongside a latent zero-masking validation in the appendix.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The core building blocks—joint multimodal self-attention (similar to MM-DiT / MMAudio) and localized region-weighted loss functions—are well-established concepts in multimodal generative modeling and talking-face synthesis, meaning the theoretical novelty is somewhat limited.

Absence of human perceptual evaluations: Assessment relies exclusively on automated heuristics (SyncNet LSE-C, Whisper WER, CLAP, MANIQA, DINO). In audio-visual generative modeling, automated metrics often correlate imperfectly with human perception; a rigorous user study evaluating perceptual naturalness, audiovisual synchrony, and speech clarity is missing.

Heavy skew toward talking-head evaluation: Although the paper describes a unified model trained on general text2audio, text2video-audio, and text2avatar-speech data, the empirical results and ablations primarily focus on avatar/talking-head generation, leaving general sound/video generation less thoroughly analyzed.

Minor presentation and editorial issues: Section 6 ends abruptly with an unfinished sentence ('...will not be integrated into any products of .'), likely caused by incomplete institutional anonymization.
